ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A small block with a charge of $+q$ and mass $m$ is placed on a smooth inclined plane with an angle of $37^{\circ}$. When the entire setup is placed in a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right, the small block remains stationary. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$, $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$.

1. What is the magnitude of the electric field strength directed horizontally to the right?
2. If the electric field strength is changed to be vertically downward with the same magnitude, what are the magnitude of the acceleration of the small block released from rest at height $H$ and the speed when it reaches the ground?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is a smooth inclined plane; the inclined plane rises from the lower left to the upper right; the angle between the inclined plane and the horizontal ground is labeled 37°; a small block is located on the inclined plane; multiple horizontal arrows in the figure point to the right and are labeled electric field E. Reasoning: Analyze along the direction of the inclined plane. The block is positively charged, so in the horizontal rightward electric field it is subjected to an electric field force qE, whose component upward along the inclined plane is qE cos37°; the component of gravity downward along the inclined plane is mg sin37°. The block is stationary, so qE cos37° = mg sin37°, obtaining E = mg tan37°/q = mg(0.6/0.8)/q = 3mg/(4q). If the electric field is changed to vertically downward and has the same magnitude, then the electric field force qE is vertically downward, in the same direction as gravity, and the total vertically downward force is mg + qE = mg + 3mg/4 = 7mg/4. Its component downward along the inclined plane is (7mg/4)sin37°, so the acceleration a = [(7mg/4)/m]sin37° = (7g/4)(0.6) = 21g/20. Sliding from height H to the ground, the displacement along the inclined plane is s = H/sin37° = H/0.6 = 5H/3. From v^2 = 2as, obtain v^2 = 2·(21g/20)·(5H/3) = 7gH/2, therefore v = sqrt(7gH/2).

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the block is on a smooth incline rising to the right, the incline makes 37° with the horizontal, and the electric field arrows point horizontally to the right. When the field is instead vertically downward with the same magnitude, the downward body force is mg + qE. Its component down the plane is (mg + qE) sin37°, so a = [(mg + qE)/m] sin37° = (g + 3g/4)(0.6) = 21g/20. From the image/text height H, the incline distance to the ground is s = H/sin37°; apply v^2 = 2as to get v = sqrt(7gH/2).

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the normal to the drawn incline is perpendicular to a plane tilted 37° above the horizontal, while the electric field lines are horizontal rightward. In the first situation, because the block is stationary and the plane is smooth, the resultant of mg downward and qE rightward must be exactly perpendicular to the incline, so it can be balanced by the normal force. Thus the tangent of the incline angle gives qE/mg = tan37° = 0.6/0.8, yielding E = 3mg/(4q). A frictionless block on a 37° incline under this effective gravity has acceleration a = g_eff sin37° = 21g/20. For the final speed, use the effective-gravity energy drop over vertical height H: v^2/2 = g_eff H, so v = sqrt(2g_eff H) = sqrt(7gH/2).

For the initial horizontal rightward field, use potential/virtual work along the allowed coordinate. 图像描述：附图中可见一条光滑斜面从左下向右上倾斜，斜面与水平地面夹角标为 37°；小带电块位于斜面上；图中多条水平箭头指向右方，表示初始电场 E 水平向右。

raw_record.original_question:
A small block with a charge of $+q$ and mass $m$ is placed on a smooth inclined plane with an angle of $37^{\circ}$. When the entire setup is placed in a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right, the small block remains stationary. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$, $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$.

1. What is the magnitude of the electric field strength directed horizontally to the right?
2. If the electric field strength is changed to be vertically downward with the same magnitude, what are the magnitude of the acceleration of the small block released from rest at height $H$ and the speed when it reaches the ground?
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is a smooth inclined plane; the inclined plane rises from the lower left to the upper right; the angle between the inclined plane and the horizontal ground is labeled 37°; a small block is located on the inclined plane; multiple horizontal arrows in the figure point to the right and are labeled electric field E. Reasoning: Analyze along the direction of the inclined plane. The block is positively charged, so in the horizontal rightward electric field it is subjected to an electric field force qE, whose component upward along the inclined plane is qE cos37°; the component of gravity downward along the inclined plane is mg sin37°. The block is stationary, so qE cos37° = mg sin37°, obtaining E = mg tan37°/q = mg(0.6/0.8)/q = 3mg/(4q). If the electric field is changed to vertically downward and has the same magnitude, then the electric field force qE is vertically downward, in the same direction as gravity, and the total vertically downward force is mg + qE = mg + 3mg/4 = 7mg/4. Its component downward along the inclined plane is (7mg/4)sin37°, so the acceleration a = [(7mg/4)/m]sin37° = (7g/4)(0.6) = 21g/20. Sliding from height H to the ground, the displacement along the inclined plane is s = H/sin37° = H/0.6 = 5H/3. From v^2 = 2as, obtain v^2 = 2·(21g/20)·(5H/3) = 7gH/2, therefore v = sqrt(7gH/2).
